En [[cib-realimentacion|el primer tema d: In [[cib-realimentacion|the first topic of the block]] we corrected with a single rule: look at how far you have drifted and push in proportion. It works, and for many things it is enough. But it has two defects that appear as soon as it is tried in the real world, and fixing them demands exactly the two tools you learnt in analysis: the [[fn-integral-def|integral]] as accumulation and the [[fn-derivadas|derivative]] as rate of change.
Este tema es, en ese sentido, el que más: This topic is, in that sense, the one that gets the most out of the whole course: you are going to see the derivative and the integral working together, in real time, to pilot something. Not as an exercise, but as the two hands you steer with.
Todo controlador vive de una sola cantid: Every controller lives off a single quantity: the difference between what you want and what there is. It is called the error signal and it is the only thing the controller looks at. It does not even need to know what it is controlling.
Se lee: <em>«e de te es igual a erre men:
Read as: “e of t equals r minus y of t”.

$r$ is the reference or set point —what you want— and $y(t)$ is the measurement —what there is at the moment $t$—.

The error being negative is no problem: it means you have overshot, and the sign is precisely what tells the controller which way to push.
A partir de esa señal se pueden hacer tr: From that signal three different questions can be asked, and each gives one term of the controller. They are these, and it is worth reading them slowly because the last three words are already familiar:
<strong>¿Cuánto me he desviado ahora mis: How far have I drifted right now? That is the error, nothing more. It gives the proportional term.
<strong>¿Cuánto error llevo acumulado de: How much error have I accumulated since I started? Adding the error over time is integrating it. It gives the integral term.
<strong>¿Hacia dónde va el error, se est: Where is the error heading, is it correcting itself or getting worse? The rate at which the error changes is its derivative. It gives the derivative term.
Se dice: <em>«u de te es igual a ka pe p:
It is said: “u of t equals K p times e of t, plus K i times the integral from zero to t of e of tau d tau, plus K d times the derivative of e with respect to time”.

The letter $\tau$ is the Greek tau and only serves to avoid repeating the $t$ inside the integral: it runs over time from the beginning until now.

The three coefficients $K_p$, $K_i$ and $K_d$ are the controls: they say how much notice to take of each term. Adjusting them is called “tuning the controller”, and it is a craft.

In plain words: “I correct according to how far off I am, plus how far off I have been in total, plus how fast the deviation is moving”.
Fíjate en lo que acaba de pasar. La inte: Notice what has just happened. The integral, which you learnt as “the area under a curve”, is here the controller's memory: it remembers all the error that has gone uncorrected. And the derivative, which you learnt as “the gradient of the tangent”, is here anticipation: if the error is falling fast, it warns that it is time to ease off before overshooting. Memory and anticipation, with the two operations of calculus.
Para esto servían: This is what they were for
Los tres términos del PID: The three terms of the PID
Cada término arregla un defecto concreto: Each term fixes a particular defect, and the best way of understanding them is to see them fail one at a time.
Hay una pregunta que conviene resolver a: There is a question worth settling before going on, because otherwise the formula and the practice look like two different things. The PID formula carries an integral and a derivative, which are operations on continuous functions. But a real controller is a device that wakes up every few milliseconds, takes one measurement and decides. It does not have the whole function in front of it. How does it integrate and differentiate something it only knows in little pieces?
La respuesta es que no lo hace: lo <stro: The answer is that it does not: it approximates it, and with the two most natural approximations there are. Let us call $\Delta t$ the time between two measurements —the step— and $e_n$ the error measured at step $n$.
la integral y la derivada, tal como las: the integral and the derivative, as a machine computes them
La primera dice: <em>«la integral del er:
The first says: “the integral of the error is approximated by the sum of all the errors measured, each multiplied by the step”. It is exactly the definition of [[fn-integral-def|the definite integral]]: the area under the curve as a sum of little rectangles of width $\Delta t$.

The second: “the derivative is approximated by the error now minus the previous one, divided by the step”. It is the difference quotient, the same one with which the derivative was defined, but without going as far as the limit: stopping at a small but real $\Delta t$.
Merece la pena apreciar lo que esto sign: It is worth appreciating what this means. A PID controller knows no infinitesimal calculus: it only adds and subtracts. What happens is that adding many little pieces resembles integrating, and subtracting two consecutive values resembles differentiating, and with a small enough step that resemblance is sufficient. All scientific computation works this way: the machine does not compute limits, it computes approximations with finite steps.
Por qué en el ejercicio se suma y se res: Why in the exercise you add and subtract
En los ejercicios de este tema el paso v: In the exercises of this topic the step is $\Delta t = 1$ so as not to drag decimals along, so the integral reduces to “the sum of the errors” and the derivative to “the error now minus the previous one”. In a real device that step is usually milliseconds, and then you do have to multiply and divide by it.
Con únicamente el término proporcional,: With the proportional term alone, the correction is proportional to the error. The problem appears when there is a constant load pushing against it —gravity on a lift, the cold coming in through the window, the weight of a drone—. To compensate for it a permanent correction is needed, and a permanent correction demands a permanent error, because the proportional term gives nothing if the error is zero.
El resultado es que el sistema se queda: The result is that the system stays almost on target, but never quite. That gap is called the steady-state error, and it is reason number one why proportional-only control is not enough.
Un dron con control solo proporcional se: A drone with proportional-only control stays a hand's breadth below the requested height and hovers there. Why does it not climb that last bit?
Porque el controlador tiene poca gananci: Because the controller has low gain; with more $K_p$ it would climb all the way
Con más $K_p$ el hueco se hace más peque: With more $K_p$ the gap becomes smaller, but never zero: to hold up the weight a permanent action is needed, and the proportional action is zero when the error is zero.
Porque sostener el peso exige una acción: Because holding up the weight demands a constant action, and with no error there is no proportional action
El dron encuentra el punto donde $K_p\\,: The drone finds the point where $K_p\,e$ exactly compensates its weight. That $e$ cannot be zero. Only the integral term, which accumulates, can give action with zero error.
Porque el sensor de altura está mal cali: Because the height sensor is badly calibrated
Puede pasar, pero no es esto: el fenómen: That can happen, but it is not this: the phenomenon appears with a perfect sensor. It is structural to proportional control against a constant load.

Calcula el error de ahora y el del paso: Compute the error now and that of the previous step. Is it rising or falling?
<strong>Proporcional.</strong> $K_p\\,e: Proportional. $K_p\,e = 2\cdot 6 = 12$. The further away, the harder it pushes.
<strong>Integral.</strong> Acumulado nue: Integral. New accumulation: $10 + 6\cdot 1 = 16$. Term: $K_i\cdot 16 = 3{.}2$. It is the memory: it carries 16 units of uncorrected error.
Suma el error de ahora al acumulado. ¿Cu: Add the error now to the accumulation. How much does the integral term contribute?
<strong>Derivativo.</strong> Variación d: Derivative. Change of the error: $(6 - 9)/1 = -3$. Term: $K_d\cdot(-3) = -3$. Negative: the error is already falling fast, so it brakes.
El error pasa de 9 a 6. ¿Qué signo tiene: The error goes from 9 to 6. What sign does the derivative have and what does the term do?

Tres preguntas sobre la misma señal: cuá: Three questions about the same signal: how much, how much so far, where it is heading. And no operation harder than adding and subtracting: the integral is a sum and the derivative, a subtraction.
El término integral: la memoria que cier: The integral term: the memory that closes the gap
La integral acumula el error. Si queda u: The integral accumulates the error. If a little gap of error is left, however small, the accumulation goes on growing without stopping and with it the correction, until the gap closes. It is stubborn: it is not satisfied with being close.
Su peligro es esa misma terquedad. Si el: Its danger is that same stubbornness. If the error persists for a long time —because the system is blocked, for example— the integral runs away and then takes an age to discharge, causing an enormous overshoot. Engineers call it windup, and every serious controller carries a limit to avoid it.
El término derivativo: el freno anticipa: The derivative term: the anticipatory brake
La derivada mira la <em>velocidad</em> d: The derivative looks at the speed of the error. If the error is closing very fast, the derivative term brakes before arriving, because it guesses that at that rate we are going to overshoot. It is what a driver does who lifts their foot before the traffic light instead of braking on top of it.
Su peligro es el ruido. Como responde al: Its danger is noise. Since it responds to the rate of change, any tremor in the measurement is amplified; that is why in practice the signal is filtered first, which is precisely the subject of another topic in this block.
Hay que llevar la barra a la línea de pu: The bar has to be brought to the dotted line, and there is a constant load pulling it down. Start with Kp only and notice that it falls short: that gap is the steady-state error. Then raise Ki and watch it close. Afterwards raise Kp a lot and add Kd to tame the overshoot.
Con $K_p = 0{,}8$ y carga 2,2, ¿cuánto e: With $K_p = 0{.}8$ and load 2.2, how much error will be left in steady state? Compute $\text{load}/K_p$. And on raising $K_p$ to 4, will the gap disappear or only shrink?

<span style=\"color:var(--warn)\">Se que: It falls short and stays there: that is the steady-state error. Raise $K_i$ and you will see it close.

<span style=\"color:var(--ok)\">Buen aju: A good setting: it reaches the target and hardly overshoots.

Un recorrido recomendado: (1) Kp=0,8 y e: A recommended route: (1) Kp=0.8 and the rest at zero. (2) Raise Ki to 0.6. (3) Raise Kp to 4 and look at the overshoot. (4) Add Kd until it is tamed.
Hay un detalle que la fórmula del PID no: There is a detail the PID formula does not mention: actuators have limits. A motor gives no more force than it gives, a valve does not open more than a hundred per cent and a radiator does not heat more than at full power. When the controller asks for more than the actuator can give, the actuator saturates: it delivers its maximum and the rest of the order is lost.
La saturación en sí no es grave. Lo grav: Saturation in itself is not serious. What is serious is what it does to the integral term. While the actuator is at its maximum and the error does not fall, the integral goes on accumulating error as if it were of any use. When the system finally responds, the integral is so charged that it keeps the actuator at maximum long after reaching the target, and the system overshoots. That is windup: the integral “winds itself up”. The simplest remedy, anti-windup, consists of stopping integrating while the actuator is saturated and the error pushes in the same direction.
La integral que no se calla: The integral that will not be quiet
El sistema está bloqueado al principio —: The system is blocked at the start —a stuck valve, a door that will not open— and cannot move even though the controller pushes with everything. Lengthen the blockage and compare the two curves: without anti-windup, the integral accumulates all that error and the system overshoots enormously when it comes free; with anti-windup, it arrives almost clean.
Si el bloqueo dura el doble, ¿el sobrepa: If the blockage lasts twice as long, will the overshoot without anti-windup be twice as big, more than twice or the same? Think about how much error the integral accumulates meanwhile.
Sintonizar sin conocer el sistema: Ziegl: Tuning without knowing the system: Ziegler-Nichols
Para ajustar $K_p$, $K_i$ y $K_d$ con cu: To set $K_p$, $K_i$ and $K_d$ by computation you need a mathematical model of the system, and often you do not have one: a factory has hundreds of control loops, each with its furnace, its pipework and its motor. In 1942, John Ziegler and Nathaniel Nichols, two engineers at a measuring instrument firm, published a recipe that needs no model, only an experiment with the real system:
Se quitan los términos integral y deriva: The integral and derivative terms are removed and only the proportional one is left.
Se sube $K_p$ poco a poco hasta que el s: $K_p$ is raised little by little until the system oscillates in a sustained way, neither growing nor dying away. That value is the ultimate gain $K_u$.
Se mide el periodo de esa oscilación: el: The period of that oscillation is measured: the ultimate period $T_u$.
Con esos dos números se leen los ajustes: With those two numbers the settings are read off the table.
de los tiempos a las ganancias: from the times to the gains
La tabla da el <strong>tiempo integral</:
The table gives the integral time $T_i$ and the derivative time $T_d$, which is how engineers prefer to think: $T_i$ is how long the integral takes to match the proportional term if the error stays constant, and $T_d$ is how far ahead the derivative looks.

To get to the gains of the PID formula, $K_i$ divides and $K_d$ multiplies.
Ziegler-Nichols da un punto de partida a: Ziegler-Nichols gives an aggressive starting point, with quite a lot of overshoot, not a final setting. And the experiment of taking the system to the edge of instability cannot be done with just anything: with a chemical reactor or an aircraft you do not experiment. For those cases you tune on a model, in simulation.
Un punto de partida, no el final: A starting point, not the end
El PID es, con diferencia, el algoritmo: The PID is by far the most used control algorithm in the world: it is estimated to govern the vast majority of industrial control loops in existence, and it has been doing so since the nineteen-forties. It is in a car's cruise control, in the oven that keeps the temperature, in a robot's arm, in the 3D printer that heats the nozzle, in a camera's stabiliser and in the four motors of a drone correcting themselves hundreds of times a second so that it stays still in the air.
El primer PID reconocible es de 1922 y s: The first recognisable PID is from 1922 and came out of a very concrete problem: governing a ship's rudder. Nicolas Minorsky, a Russian engineer who had emigrated to the United States, was studying how expert helmsmen steered and observed that they reacted not only to the wrong heading, but also to the persistence of the drift and to the speed at which the ship was turning. He wrote that down in equations and obtained the three terms. That is: the PID was not invented in a laboratory, it was copied by observing people who already did it well without knowing they did.
Y esa historia tiene una lectura que va: And that story has a reading that goes beyond engineering: the way a person regulates something fluently usually contains, unformulated, the right mathematics. The same happens when learning to drive, to pour water without spilling it or to balance on a bicycle: what is being acquired with practice is a tuning of gains.

Lo reduce a $\\text{carga}/K_p$, pero nu: It reduces it to $\text{load}/K_p$, but never cancels it, and a very high $K_p$ oscillates. The gap is closed by the integral term.
Derivar la medida en vez del error: Differentiating the measurement instead of the error
El término derivativo usa $e_n - e_{n-1}: The derivative term uses $e_n - e_{n-1}$. With a constant reference it coincides with $-(y_n - y_{n-1})$, but the sign changes: you have to be careful.
Dejar integrar mientras el actuador está: Letting it integrate while the actuator is saturated
La integral se carga con error que no pu: The integral charges up with error it cannot correct and then causes an enormous overshoot. That is windup, and every serious PID carries a limit.
Tomar Ziegler-Nichols como ajuste final: Taking Ziegler-Nichols as the final setting
Da un punto de partida agresivo, con sob: It gives an aggressive starting point, with overshoot. And the experiment of taking the system to the edge of oscillation cannot be done with a reactor or an aircraft.
Ojo con la derivada: es la variación del: Careful with the derivative: it is the change of the error, not of the measurement. And the previous error is computed the same way, with the previous measurement.

Hay sobrepaso y oscilación: falta el tér: There is overshoot and oscillation: the term that brakes before arriving is missing.

La respuesta inmediata es floja: hay que: The immediate response is weak: the proportional gain has to be raised.
El dron se queda un palmo por debajo de: The drone stays a hand's breadth below the requested height and climbs no further.
La carga constante (el peso) exige una c: The constant load (the weight) demands a permanent correction, and only the accumulator gives that.

Con error grande debería haber acción gr: With a large error there should be a large action: that is the proportional term.
Fíjate en QUÉ falla, no en cuánto. ¿Se q: Look at WHAT fails, not at how much. Is a gap left that nobody closes? Does it arrive but overshooting and coming back? Or does it simply react listlessly? Each symptom points at a different term, and you have already seen which fixes what.

Con solo el término proporcional, el err: With the proportional term alone, the steady-state error against a load is $\frac{\text{load}}{K_p}$: it falls as $K_p$ rises, but it does not disappear.
